YK-11 | Myostatin Inhibitor for Extreme Muscle Growth

claims.statement: YK-11 is not an FDA-approved drug or approved supplement ingredient. FDA laboratory testing of a bodybuilding product (GE Labs Ykarine) confirmed it contained YK-11 as a listed ingredient alongside undeclared trendione (an anabolic steroid), and FDA's investigation was prompted by an adverse event report of a consumer who used the product and subsequently suffered a stroke.

context.formulation: commercial bodybuilding product (GE Labs Ykarine) containing YK-11
context.useCase: regulatory safety warning / adulterated product enforcement

extractedEvidence.quote: The laboratory analysis also confirmed the product contains YK-11, which is a listed ingredient on the product label.
The testing found the product contained undeclared trendione (estra-4,9,11-triene-3,17-dione), which is an anabolic steroid.
The agency testing was based on an adverse event report of a consumer who used the product and subsequently suffered a stroke.
Life-threatening reactions, including liver injuries that required hospitalization, have occurred in people taking products containing SARMs.

reviewFlags: adverse event (stroke) is associated with a combination product (YK-11 plus undeclared trendione), not YK-11 in isolation; causal attribution to YK-11 alone is not established

claims.statement: NIH LiverTox describes YK-11 as a steroidal SARM/myostatin inhibitor not approved for human use, banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and implicated (typically in combination with other SARMs) in cases of clinically apparent liver injury with cholestatic/jaundice patterns resembling anabolic-steroid-induced liver injury; a cited case involved a 23-year-old who developed jaundice three months after starting three SARMs (including ligandrol, testolone, and YK-11), with bilirubin peaking at 36.4 mg/dL and slow recovery over three months.

context.population: recreational bodybuilding users of multi-SARM stacks
context.formulation: research-chemical YK-11, usually combined with other SARMs

YK-11, like anabolic steroids and the nonsteroidal SARMS, is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency.
have been implicated in multiple cases of severe cholestatic jaundice that resembles anabolic steroid jaundice.

claims.statement: YK-11 is described as a gene-selective/steroidal partial agonist of the androgen receptor that, at low concentration, activates AR transcriptional activity and accelerates nuclear translocation of the receptor without inducing the N-terminal/C-terminal (N/C) interaction typical of full agonists; it also acts as a myostatin-pathway inhibitor, increasing follistatin and myogenic regulatory factor (MyoD, Myf5, myogenin) expression in cultured muscle cells.

claims.statement: In an in vitro study using MC3T3-E1 mouse osteoblast cells, YK-11 (like dihydrotestosterone) accelerated cell proliferation and mineralization and increased osteoblast differentiation markers (osteoprotegerin, osteocalcin); effects were attenuated by an androgen-receptor antagonist and were associated with increased phosphorylated Akt, suggesting a non-genomic AR-signaling component.

context.population: in vitro mouse osteoblast cell line (not human, not in vivo)

extractedEvidence.quote: treatment of YK11 and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) accelerated cell proliferation and mineralization in MC3T3-E1 mouse osteoblast cells. Further, YK11-treated cells increased osteoblast specific differentiation markers, such as osteoprotegerin and osteocalcin, compared to untreated cells. These observations were attenuated by androgen receptor (AR) antagonist treatment.
The phosphorylated Akt protein level was increased by YK11 and DHT treatment, suggesting that YK11 activates Akt-signaling via non-genomic signaling of AR.

reviewFlags: in vitro rodent cell-line finding only; must not be extrapolated to human bone or muscle outcomes

claims.statement: No published human clinical trials of YK-11 were identified in this review. All mechanistic and efficacy evidence located is preclinical (cell culture and animal models); human pharmacokinetics, dosing, efficacy for muscle growth, and long-term safety in people are unestablished.

claims.statement: YK-11 is marketed online with superlative human-benefit language (e.g., 'extreme muscle growth,' 'incredible muscle fullness,' testimonial claims of fast strength gains) despite vendor pages themselves acknowledging no controlled clinical evidence supports these outcomes; the marketing channel (customer testimonials implying personal use) is in tension with 'research use only' labeling on the same product.

conflicts.summary: Both documented human harm signals for YK-11 (the FDA stroke adverse-event report and the LiverTox jaundice case) involve YK-11 used in combination with other undeclared or co-administered agents (trendione; ligandrol and testolone respectively), so neither source isolates YK-11 as the sole causal agent. Marketing sources present YK-11 as if its effects and safety profile were independently characterized in humans, which the regulatory/clinical sources do not support.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

PubMed abstract pages (23995658, 38521455, 30379415) returned reCAPTCHA/robots-blocked content to automated fetch this session; primary-literature quotes for the original Kanno et al. 2011/2013 mechanism papers and the hippocampal oxidative-stress rodent studies were not independently re-verified from the primary journal source and are currently sourced via a vendor technical datasheet (Cayman Chemical) instead.
PubChem CID (119058028) and CAS number were cross-confirmed across PubChem, Cayman Chemical, and MedKoo vendor pages but ChEMBL/UNII/DrugBank identifiers remain unresolved.

No dedicated YK-11-only human case series or controlled human study was located; human safety/efficacy evidence rests entirely on multi-SARM case reports and a single FDA adulterated-product adverse-event report.
Vendor/marketing landscape for YK-11 changes frequently (product reformulations, delisting); marketing claim example should be re-checked for currency at each review cycle.
